questions.question: What percentage of base sequences is identical among all humans?
questions.explanation: According to the text, 99.9 percent of nucleotide bases are exactly the same in all humans. Only 0.1% differs, which accounts for individual uniqueness.

questions.question: What makes every individual unique in their phenotypic appearance?
questions.explanation: The text states that differences in sequence of DNA make every individual unique in their phenotypic appearance. These variations account for physical and genetic diversity.

questions.question: What is DNA fingerprinting primarily used for?
questions.explanation: DNA fingerprinting is described as a very quick way to compare the DNA sequences of any two individuals. It helps identify genetic differences without sequencing entire genomes.

questions.question: What are repetitive DNA sequences?
options: DNA sequences that are repeated many times
questions.explanation: Repetitive DNA refers to specific regions in DNA sequence where a small stretch of DNA is repeated many times. These regions are crucial for DNA fingerprinting analysis.

questions.question: How is satellite DNA separated from bulk genomic DNA?
questions.explanation: Satellite DNA is separated from bulk genomic DNA as different peaks during density gradient centrifugation. The bulk DNA forms a major peak while satellite DNA appears as smaller peaks.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a category of satellite DNA?
options: Both A and B are categories
questions.explanation: The text mentions that satellite DNA is classified into categories such as micro-satellites and mini-satellites based on base composition, length, and number of repetitive units. Macro-satellites are not mentioned.

questions.question: Do repetitive DNA sequences code for proteins?
options: Yes, they code for essential proteins
No, they do not code for any proteins
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states that these repetitive sequences normally do not code for any proteins. However, they form a large portion of the human genome and show high polymorphism.

questions.question: What property of repetitive DNA sequences makes them useful for DNA fingerprinting?
options: They are identical in all individuals
They show high degree of polymorphism
They are found only in blood cells
questions.explanation: The text states that these sequences show high degree of polymorphism and form the basis of DNA fingerprinting. This variation allows identification of individuals.

questions.question: Which tissues from an individual can be used for DNA fingerprinting?
options: Blood, hair follicle, skin, bone, saliva, and sperm
questions.explanation: The text lists multiple tissues: blood, hair-follicle, skin, bone, saliva, and sperm. DNA from every tissue shows the same degree of polymorphism, making them useful identification tools.

questions.question: What causes DNA polymorphism?
questions.explanation: The text states that polymorphism arises due to mutations. New mutations may arise in somatic cells or germ cells, and if transmitted to offspring, they can spread in the population.

questions.question: What is the minimum frequency of a variant allele to be considered a DNA polymorphism?
questions.explanation: The text defines DNA polymorphism as an allelic sequence variation where more than one variant at a locus occurs in human population with a frequency greater than 0.01.

questions.question: Why is the probability of observing polymorphism higher in noncoding DNA sequences?
options: Mutations in these sequences may not affect reproductive ability
questions.explanation: The text explains that mutations in noncoding DNA sequences may not have any immediate effect on an individual's reproductive ability, so these mutations accumulate and form variability.

questions.question: What role do polymorphisms play in evolution and speciation?
options: They play a very important role
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states that for evolution and speciation, such polymorphisms play a very important role. Genetic variation is the raw material for natural selection and adaptation.

questions.question: Where can new mutations arise in an individual?
options: In somatic cells or germ cells
questions.explanation: The text states that new mutations may arise in an individual either in somatic cells or in germ cells. Only germ cell mutations can be transmitted to offspring through sexual reproduction.

questions.question: What happens if a germ cell mutation does not impair reproductive ability?
options: It can spread to other members of the population
questions.explanation: The text explains that if a germ cell mutation does not seriously impair the individual's ability to have offspring who can transmit the mutation, it can spread to other members of the population through sexual reproduction.

questions.question: What is the range of polymorphism types mentioned in the text?
options: From single nucleotide change to very large scale changes
questions.explanation: The text mentions a variety of different types of polymorphisms ranging from single nucleotide change to very large scale changes. This spectrum of variation contributes to genetic diversity.

questions.question: According to the RNA World hypothesis, which molecule was the first genetic material?
questions.explanation: RNA was the first genetic material. There is now enough evidence to suggest that essential life processes such as metabolism, translation, and splicing evolved around RNA.

questions.question: What dual role did RNA play in early life according to the RNA World concept?
questions.explanation: RNA used to act as a genetic material as well as a catalyst. There are some important biochemical reactions in living systems that are catalyzed by RNA catalysts and not by protein enzymes.

questions.question: Why did DNA evolve from RNA according to the text?
options: DNA is more reactive than RNA
RNA being a catalyst was reactive and hence unstable
RNA could not store genetic information
questions.explanation: RNA being a catalyst was reactive and hence unstable. Therefore, DNA has evolved from RNA with chemical modifications that make it more stable.

questions.question: What feature of DNA makes it more resistant to changes compared to RNA?
options: Presence of uracil instead of thymine
questions.explanation: DNA being double stranded and having complementary strand further resists changes by evolving a process of repair.

questions.question: What scheme did Watson and Crick propose for DNA replication?
questions.explanation: Watson and Crick proposed a scheme where the two strands would separate and act as a template for synthesis of new complementary strands. After replication, each DNA molecule would have one parental and one newly synthesized strand. This was termed semiconservative DNA replication.

questions.question: In the Meselson-Stahl experiment, what isotope was used to label DNA?
questions.explanation: They grew E. coli in a medium containing 15NH4Cl (15N is the heavy isotope of nitrogen) as the only nitrogen source. This heavy DNA molecule could be distinguished from normal DNA by centrifugation in a cesium chloride density gradient.

questions.question: What was the density of DNA after one generation in the Meselson-Stahl experiment?
questions.explanation: The DNA extracted from the culture one generation after transfer from 15N to 14N medium had a hybrid or intermediate density.

questions.question: After two generations in the Meselson-Stahl experiment, what was the composition of DNA?
options: Equal amounts of hybrid DNA and light DNA
questions.explanation: DNA extracted after another generation was composed of equal amounts of hybrid DNA and light DNA.

questions.question: Which organism was used by Taylor and colleagues to prove semiconservative replication in chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Very similar experiments involving use of radioactive thymidine to detect distribution of newly synthesized DNA in chromosomes was performed on Vicia faba (faba beans) by Taylor and colleagues in 1958.

questions.question: What method was used to separate DNA molecules based on density in the Meselson-Stahl experiment?
questions.explanation: The heavy DNA molecule could be distinguished from the normal DNA by centrifugation in a cesium chloride (CsCl) density gradient.

questions.question: Which enzyme is primarily responsible for catalyzing DNA replication?
questions.explanation: The main enzyme is referred to as DNA-dependent DNA polymerase, since it uses a DNA template to catalyze the polymerization of deoxynucleotides.

questions.question: In which direction does DNA polymerase catalyze polymerization?
questions.explanation: The DNA-dependent DNA polymerases catalyze polymerization only in one direction, that is 5' to 3'.

questions.question: What are the fragments called that are synthesized discontinuously during DNA replication?
questions.explanation: The discontinuously synthesized fragments are later joined by the enzyme DNA ligase. These are known as Okazaki fragments.

questions.question: What is the region in DNA where replication originates called?
questions.explanation: There is a definite region in E. coli DNA where the replication originates. Such regions are termed as origin of replication.

questions.question: During which phase of the cell cycle does DNA replication occur in eukaryotes?
questions.explanation: In eukaryotes, the replication of DNA takes place at S-phase of the cell-cycle.

questions.question: How many codons code for amino acids according to the genetic code?
questions.explanation: Out of 64 possible codons (4^3), 61 codons code for amino acids while 3 codons function as stop codons.

questions.question: Which codons function as stop codons in the genetic code?
questions.explanation: UAA, UAG, and UGA are the three stop or terminator codons that do not code for any amino acid.

questions.question: What does the term 'degenerate' mean in the context of genetic code?
options: The code is read with punctuation marks
Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon
The code varies between different organisms
Only one codon exists for each amino acid
questions.explanation: The genetic code is degenerate because some amino acids are coded by more than one codon. For example, multiple codons can code for the same amino acid.

questions.question: Which property of genetic code states that the code is read without any punctuation?
questions.explanation: The codon is read in mRNA in a contiguous fashion, meaning there are no punctuations between codons. The reading frame continues without interruption.

questions.question: What is the dual function of the AUG codon?
options: It codes for Alanine and acts as a stop codon
It codes for Methionine and acts as an initiator codon
It codes for Phenylalanine and acts as a terminator
It codes for Tryptophan and acts as a regulator
questions.explanation: AUG has dual functions: it codes for Methionine (met) and it also acts as the initiator codon that signals the start of protein synthesis.

questions.question: The genetic code is described as nearly universal. What does this mean?
options: The code is identical in all organisms without any exceptions
The same codon codes for the same amino acid from bacteria to humans with few exceptions
The code changes completely in different species
Only eukaryotes share the same genetic code
questions.explanation: The genetic code is nearly universal, meaning the same codon codes for the same amino acid across most organisms. For example, UUU codes for Phenylalanine from bacteria to humans. Some exceptions exist in mitochondrial codons and some protozoans.

questions.question: For the mRNA sequence AUG UUU UUC UUC UUU UUU UUC, what is the first amino acid in the polypeptide chain?
questions.explanation: AUG is the initiator codon that codes for Methionine. Therefore, the first amino acid in the polypeptide chain would be Methionine.

questions.question: Which amino acid is coded by the codon UUU?
questions.explanation: UUU codes for Phenylalanine (Phe). This is a standard example used to illustrate the universality of the genetic code.

questions.question: Why is it difficult to predict the mRNA sequence from a given amino acid sequence?
options: Because the genetic code is not universal
Because of the degeneracy of the genetic code
Because there are no stop codons
Because amino acids do not bind to tRNA
questions.explanation: Due to the degeneracy of the genetic code, multiple codons can code for the same amino acid. Therefore, knowing the amino acid sequence does not uniquely determine the mRNA sequence.

questions.question: What is the total number of possible codons in the genetic code?
questions.explanation: Since there are 4 bases and each codon consists of 3 nucleotides, the total number of possible codons is 4^3 = 64.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a property of the genetic code?
questions.explanation: The genetic code is read in a contiguous fashion without any punctuations. The other options (triplet, degenerate, nearly universal) are all established properties of the genetic code.

questions.question: In the mRNA sequence AUG UUU UUC UUC UUU UUU UUC, how many times does Phenylalanine appear?
questions.explanation: After the initiator AUG (Methionine), the sequence contains UUU, UUC, UUC, UUU, UUU, UUC. Both UUU and UUC code for Phenylalanine, so Phenylalanine appears 6 times in total.

questions.question: Where are exceptions to the universal genetic code commonly found?
options: In mitochondrial codons and some protozoans
questions.explanation: Exceptions to the universal genetic code have been found in mitochondrial codons and in some protozoans. These are specific cases where the standard code is slightly modified.

questions.question: What does the term 'triplet' mean regarding the genetic code?
options: Each codon consists of three nucleotides
There are three types of genetic codes
Each amino acid is coded by exactly three codons
The code has three stop codons only
questions.explanation: The genetic code is triplet, meaning each codon consists of three nucleotides. This was proposed by George Gamow, who calculated that 4^3 = 64 codons would be sufficient to code for 20 amino acids.

questions.question: For the amino acid sequence Met-Phe-Phe-Phe-Phe-Phe-Phe, which codon must definitely be present?
questions.explanation: AUG is the only codon that codes for Methionine and also serves as the initiator codon. Since the sequence starts with Methionine, AUG must be present. UUU and UUC both code for Phenylalanine, so either or both could be used.

questions.question: Which two properties of the genetic code are demonstrated when predicting an amino acid sequence from mRNA versus predicting mRNA from an amino acid sequence?
questions.explanation: Predicting amino acids from mRNA is straightforward due to universality, but predicting mRNA from amino acids is difficult due to degeneracy (multiple codons for same amino acid). These two properties are highlighted in this exercise.

questions.question: How many stop codons are present in the genetic code?
questions.explanation: There are 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) that do not code for any amino acid. These signal the termination of protein synthesis.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of nucleotides required to code for one amino acid?
questions.explanation: The genetic code is a triplet code, meaning a minimum of 3 nucleotides (one codon) is required to code for one amino acid. With only 4 bases, 2 nucleotides would only give 16 combinations (4^2), which is insufficient for 20 amino acids.

questions.question: Which scientist proposed that the genetic code should be made up of three nucleotides to code for 20 amino acids?
questions.explanation: George Gamow, a physicist, proposed that the genetic code should be a triplet code made up of three nucleotides, as 4^3 = 64 codons would be sufficient to code for 20 amino acids.

questions.question: If a mutation changes a single nucleotide in a codon but the same amino acid is still produced, what property of the genetic code is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: This demonstrates degeneracy, where multiple codons can code for the same amino acid. A mutation in the third position of a codon often does not change the amino acid due to this redundancy.

questions.question: What role did Francis Crick propose for tRNA before the genetic code was deciphered?
options: To directly synthesize proteins without mRNA
To act as an adapter molecule linking codons to amino acids
To serve as the primary genetic material
questions.explanation: Francis Crick postulated that an adapter molecule must exist to read the genetic code and link it to specific amino acids, since amino acids lack structural features to directly read the code. This adapter function was later assigned to tRNA.

questions.question: Which part of tRNA contains bases complementary to the mRNA codon?
questions.explanation: The anticodon loop of tRNA contains three bases that are complementary to the codon on mRNA. This complementarity allows tRNA to correctly pair with the appropriate codon during translation.

questions.question: Where on the tRNA molecule is the amino acid attached?
options: At the 3' end (amino acid acceptor end)
questions.explanation: The amino acid is attached to the amino acid acceptor end of tRNA, which is located at the 3' end. This end has the sequence CCA where the amino acid binds.

questions.question: Are tRNAs specific for each amino acid?
options: No, one tRNA can carry multiple amino acids
Yes, tRNAs are specific for each amino acid
questions.explanation: tRNAs are specific for each amino acid. Each type of tRNA can only carry one specific amino acid, ensuring accuracy during protein synthesis.

questions.question: What is special about the initiator tRNA?
options: It carries two amino acids simultaneously
It is used specifically for initiation of translation
questions.explanation: The initiator tRNA is a specific tRNA that is used to start the translation process. It carries methionine (or formylmethionine in bacteria) and recognizes the start codon AUG.

questions.question: Which statement about stop codons is correct?
options: There are tRNAs for all stop codons
There are no tRNAs for stop codons
Stop codons code for special amino acids
Stop codons are recognized by ribosomal RNA only
questions.explanation: There are no tRNAs for stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA). Stop codons are recognized by release factors, not tRNAs, which signal the termination of translation.

questions.question: What does the secondary structure of tRNA resemble?
questions.explanation: The secondary structure of tRNA is depicted as a clover-leaf shape with four main arms: the acceptor arm, D-arm, anticodon arm, and T-arm.

questions.question: What is the actual three-dimensional structure of tRNA described as?
questions.explanation: In its actual three-dimensional structure, tRNA is a compact molecule that looks like an inverted L. This structure allows it to fit into the ribosome during translation.

questions.question: What is translation in molecular biology?
options: Polymerization of amino acids to form a polypeptide
questions.explanation: Translation refers to the process of polymerization of amino acids to form a polypeptide. The sequence of amino acids is determined by the sequence of bases in mRNA.

questions.question: What type of bond joins amino acids during translation?
questions.explanation: Amino acids are joined by a peptide bond during translation. This bond forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another, with the release of water.

questions.question: What provides energy for peptide bond formation during translation?
questions.explanation: Formation of a peptide bond requires energy. In the first phase, amino acids are activated in the presence of ATP and linked to their cognate tRNA in a process called charging or aminoacylation.

questions.question: What is the process called when amino acids are linked to tRNA?
questions.explanation: The process of linking amino acids to their specific tRNAs is called charging of tRNA or aminoacylation of tRNA. This requires ATP and specific aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase enzymes.

questions.question: Why must gene expression be tightly regulated?
options: Because transcription and translation are energetically expensive processes
Because RNA is not needed by the cell
questions.explanation: Transcription and translation are energetically very expensive processes. Therefore, these processes must be tightly regulated to conserve cellular energy and produce proteins only when needed.

questions.question: What is the function of beta-galactosidase in E. coli?
options: To catalyze hydrolysis of lactose into galactose and glucose
questions.explanation: Beta-galactosidase is an enzyme synthesized by E. coli that catalyzes the hydrolysis of the disaccharide lactose into its monomeric units, galactose and glucose, which the bacteria use as an energy source.

questions.question: When would E. coli no longer require synthesis of beta-galactosidase?
options: When glucose is present instead of lactose
When lactose is not available as an energy source
questions.explanation: If the bacteria do not have lactose around them to be utilized for energy source, they would no longer require the synthesis of the enzyme beta-galactosidase. This is because the enzyme is specifically needed to break down lactose.

questions.question: In prokaryotes, what is the predominant site for control of gene expression?
questions.explanation: In prokaryotes, control of the rate of transcriptional initiation is the predominant site for control of gene expression. This is where RNA polymerase activity is regulated by accessory proteins.

questions.question: How do regulatory proteins affect RNA polymerase in prokaryotes?
options: They affect its ability to recognize start sites
They have no effect on RNA polymerase
questions.explanation: Regulatory proteins can act both positively (activators) and negatively (repressors) by affecting the ability of RNA polymerase to recognize start sites. This controls whether transcription begins or not.

questions.question: What is the operator region in prokaryotic gene regulation?
options: A region that codes for proteins
A region adjacent to the promoter where repressor proteins bind
A region that initiates DNA replication
questions.explanation: The operator region is adjacent to the promoter elements in most operons. In most cases, the sequences of the operator bind a repressor protein, preventing RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon.

questions.question: Which statement about operon specificity is correct?
options: All operons share the same operator and repressor
Each operon has its specific operator and specific repressor
Operators are not specific to any operon
Repressors can bind to any operator
questions.explanation: Each operon has its specific operator and specific repressor. For example, the lac operator is present only in the lac operon and it interacts specifically with lac repressor only.

questions.question: Who elucidated the lac operon?
questions.explanation: The lac operon was elucidated by Francois Jacob, a geneticist, and Jacques Monod, a biochemist. They were the first to elucidate a transcriptionally regulated system.

questions.question: What does 'lac' in lac operon refer to?
questions.explanation: In lac operon, 'lac' refers to lactose. The lac operon codes for genes responsible for metabolism of lactose in bacteria.

questions.question: What is an operon?
options: A single gene that codes for one protein
A polycistronic structural gene regulated by a common promoter and regulatory genes
questions.explanation: An operon is a polycistronic structural gene regulated by a common promoter and regulatory genes. This arrangement is very common in bacteria.

questions.question: How many structural genes are in the lac operon?
questions.explanation: The lac operon consists of one regulatory gene (i gene) and three structural genes (z, y, and a). The z gene codes for beta-galactosidase, y for permease, and a for transacetylase.

questions.question: What does the i gene in the lac operon code for?
options: The repressor of the lac operon
questions.explanation: The i gene codes for the repressor of the lac operon. This repressor protein binds to the operator region and prevents transcription of the structural genes.

questions.question: What enzyme is coded by the z gene in the lac operon?
questions.explanation: The z gene codes for beta-galactosidase, which is primarily responsible for the hydrolysis of lactose into galactose and glucose.

questions.question: What is the function of the protein coded by the y gene in the lac operon?
options: To increase cell permeability to beta-galactosides
questions.explanation: The y gene codes for permease, which increases the permeability of the cell to beta-galactosides, allowing lactose to enter the cell.

questions.question: What enzyme is coded by the a gene in the lac operon?
questions.explanation: The a gene encodes transacetylase. All three gene products (beta-galactosidase, permease, and transacetylase) are required for metabolism of lactose.

questions.question: What is the inducer in the lac operon?
questions.explanation: Lactose is the substrate for beta-galactosidase and it regulates switching on and off of the operon. Hence, it is termed as the inducer.

questions.question: Can glucose or galactose act as inducers for the lac operon?
options: No, neither can act as inducers
questions.explanation: Glucose or galactose cannot act as inducers for the lac operon. Only lactose (or its isomer allolactose) can act as the inducer.

questions.question: What is the regulation of lac operon by repressor called?
questions.explanation: Regulation of lac operon by repressor is referred to as negative regulation because the repressor prevents transcription by binding to the operator.

questions.question: What type of mutation is caused by a change of a single base pair in the gene for beta globin chain?
questions.explanation: A point mutation is a change in a single base pair of DNA. In the case of sickle cell anemia, a single base pair change in the beta globin gene results in the substitution of amino acid glutamate with valine.

questions.question: Which amino acid is replaced in sickle cell anemia due to the point mutation in the beta globin gene?
questions.explanation: The point mutation in the beta globin gene changes the amino acid glutamate to valine, resulting in sickle cell anemia. This is a classical example of how a single base change can alter protein function and cause disease.

questions.question: What disease is caused by the point mutation that changes glutamate to valine in the beta globin chain?
questions.explanation: Sickle cell anemia is caused by a point mutation in the beta globin gene where glutamate is replaced by valine. This changes the shape of red blood cells from normal biconcave discs to sickle-shaped cells, causing various health complications.

questions.question: What happens to the reading frame when one or two bases are inserted or deleted in a structural gene?
options: The reading frame changes from the point of insertion or deletion
Only one amino acid is affected
questions.explanation: Insertion or deletion of one or two bases changes the reading frame from the point of insertion or deletion. These are called frameshift mutations because they shift the triplet reading frame, altering all subsequent amino acids in the protein sequence.

questions.question: What is the term for mutations caused by insertion or deletion of one or two bases?
questions.explanation: Frameshift insertion or deletion mutations occur when one or two bases are inserted or deleted. This changes the reading frame from the point of mutation, causing completely different amino acids to be incorporated into the protein from that point onward.

questions.question: What happens when three or multiple of three bases are inserted or deleted in a gene?
options: One or multiple amino acids are inserted or deleted, but reading frame remains unaltered
No change occurs in the protein product
questions.explanation: Insertion or deletion of three or its multiple bases inserts or deletes one or multiple codons, hence one or multiple amino acids, but the reading frame remains unaltered from that point onwards. This is less disruptive than frameshift mutations.

questions.question: In the textbook example, what is the original statement used to demonstrate reading frames?
options: THE CAT SAT ON THE MAT
questions.explanation: The textbook uses the statement 'RAM HAS RED CAP' where each word has three letters, similar to codons having three bases. This analogy helps students understand how insertion or deletion of letters (bases) changes the reading frame and produces completely different words (amino acids).

questions.question: If the letter 'B' is inserted between 'HAS' and 'RED' in 'RAM HAS RED CAP', what does the statement become?
questions.explanation: When 'B' is inserted between 'HAS' and 'RED', the reading frame shifts. The statement becomes 'RAM HAS BRE DCA P' where the three-letter word pattern is disrupted, producing meaningless words. This demonstrates how a single base insertion causes frameshift mutation.

questions.question: If two letters 'BI' are inserted between 'HAS' and 'RED' in 'RAM HAS RED CAP', what is the result?
questions.explanation: Inserting two letters 'BI' between 'HAS' and 'RED' changes the reading frame to 'RAM HAS BIR EDC AP'. This demonstrates that insertion of two bases (not divisible by 3) also causes frameshift mutation, altering all subsequent codons.

questions.question: If three letters 'BIG' are inserted between 'HAS' and 'RED' in 'RAM HAS RED CAP', what is the outcome?
options: The reading frame changes after the insertion point
The reading frame remains unchanged and the statement reads 'RAM HAS BIG RED CAP'
Only one letter is affected in the original message
questions.explanation: When three letters (a multiple of 3) are inserted, the reading frame remains unchanged. The statement becomes 'RAM HAS BIG RED CAP' which still makes sense with the original three-letter word pattern intact. This demonstrates that insertion of 3 or multiple of 3 bases adds amino acids without changing the reading frame.

questions.question: What is the effect of deleting one letter 'R' from 'RAM HAS RED CAP'?
options: The reading frame remains the same
The reading frame changes from the deletion point
Only the first word is affected
No change occurs in the message
questions.explanation: Deleting one letter (one base) from the sequence changes the reading frame from the point of deletion. Using the analogy, if 'R' is deleted from 'RED', the subsequent letters regroup into different three-letter combinations, demonstrating frameshift deletion mutation.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why the 'RAM HAS RED CAP' analogy is used in genetics?
options: To illustrate how frameshift mutations alter protein synthesis
questions.explanation: The 'RAM HAS RED CAP' analogy is used to illustrate frameshift mutations. Each three-letter word represents a codon (three bases). Inserting or deleting letters that are not multiples of 3 shifts the reading frame, just as inserting or deleting bases shifts the codon reading frame during protein synthesis.

questions.question: What is the key difference between point mutations and frameshift mutations?
options: Point mutations affect only one amino acid while frameshift mutations affect all amino acids after the mutation point
Point mutations are larger than frameshift mutations
Frameshift mutations occur only in RNA
Point mutations always cause more severe effects
questions.explanation: Point mutations change a single base pair, usually affecting only one amino acid (or sometimes none if silent). Frameshift mutations, caused by insertion or deletion of bases not divisible by 3, shift the entire reading frame, altering all amino acids from the mutation point onward, typically causing more severe effects.

questions.question: In the context of genetic mutations, what does 'reading frame' refer to?
options: The frame used to read DNA under a microscope
The grouping of bases into consecutive triplets (codons) that specify amino acids
The frame that holds the DNA double helix
The reading speed of DNA polymerase
questions.explanation: The reading frame refers to the way the sequence of bases in mRNA is grouped into consecutive non-overlapping triplets called codons. Each codon specifies one amino acid. A frameshift mutation disrupts this grouping, causing completely different amino acids to be read from the mutation point onward.

questions.question: Why are frameshift mutations generally more harmful than point mutations?
options: Because they affect only the start codon
Because they alter all amino acids from the mutation point onward and often create premature stop codons
Because they occur more frequently in nature
Because they only affect non-coding regions
questions.explanation: Frameshift mutations are more harmful because shifting the reading frame changes every subsequent codon, producing a completely different protein sequence from the mutation point. They also often create premature stop codons, truncating the protein. Point mutations usually affect only one amino acid.

questions.question: If a deletion removes exactly three bases from the middle of a gene, what is the expected outcome?
options: A frameshift mutation affecting all downstream amino acids
Deletion of exactly one amino acid from the protein with the reading frame preserved
The protein becomes twice as long
No effect on the protein product
questions.explanation: Deletion of exactly three bases (one codon) removes exactly one amino acid from the protein product. Since 3 is divisible by 3, the reading frame remains preserved. All other codons downstream are read correctly, though one amino acid is missing. This is less disruptive than frameshift mutations.

questions.question: What type of mutation occurs when a single base change results in a different amino acid being incorporated?
questions.explanation: A missense mutation is a point mutation where a single base change results in a different amino acid being incorporated into the protein. The sickle cell anemia mutation (glutamate to valine) is a classic example of a missense mutation.

questions.question: Which experimental method was instrumental in synthesizing RNA molecules with defined combinations of bases for genetic code studies?
options: Chemical method developed by Har Gobind Khorana
questions.explanation: The chemical method developed by Har Gobind Khorana was instrumental in synthesizing RNA molecules with defined combinations of bases (homopolymers and copolymers). This was crucial for deciphering the genetic code and understanding how codons specify amino acids.

questions.question: What process requires transfer of genetic information from a polymer of nucleotides to synthesise a polymer of amino acids?
questions.explanation: Translation is the process that requires transfer of genetic information from a polymer of nucleotides (mRNA) to synthesise a polymer of amino acids (proteins).

questions.question: Does any complementarity exist between nucleotides and amino acids?
questions.explanation: No complementarity exists between nucleotides and amino acids, nor could any be drawn theoretically. This is why a genetic code was proposed.

questions.question: Who argued that the genetic code should be made up of three nucleotides to code for 20 amino acids?
questions.explanation: George Gamow, a physicist, argued that since there are only 4 bases and if they have to code for 20 amino acids, the code should constitute a combination of three nucleotides.

questions.question: How many codons are generated by a permutation combination of 4^3 (4 x 4 x 4)?
questions.explanation: A permutation combination of 4^3 (4 x 4 x 4) generates 64 codons, which is more than the 20 amino acids needed.

questions.question: Which scientist developed the chemical method for synthesising RNA molecules with defined combinations of bases?
questions.explanation: Har Gobind Khorana developed the chemical method instrumental in synthesising RNA molecules with defined combinations of bases (homopolymers and copolymers).

questions.question: Whose cell-free system for protein synthesis helped decipher the genetic code?
questions.explanation: Marshall Nirenberg's cell-free system for protein synthesis finally helped the genetic code to be deciphered.

questions.question: Which enzyme was helpful in polymerising RNA with defined sequences in a template-independent manner?
questions.explanation: Severo Ochoa enzyme (polynucleotide phosphorylase) was helpful in polymerising RNA with defined sequences in a template-independent manner (enzymatic synthesis of RNA).

questions.question: How many codons code for amino acids?
questions.explanation: 61 codons code for amino acids and 3 codons do not code for any amino acids, hence they function as stop codons.

questions.question: What is the term for the property where some amino acids are coded by more than one codon?
questions.explanation: Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon, hence the code is degenerate. This means multiple codons can specify the same amino acid.

questions.question: How is the codon read in mRNA?
options: In a non-contiguous fashion with gaps
In a contiguous fashion with no punctuations
questions.explanation: The codon is read in mRNA in a contiguous fashion. There are no punctuations between codons.

questions.question: Which codon codes for Phenylalanine (Phe) from bacteria to humans?
questions.explanation: UUU would code for Phenylalanine (phe) from bacteria to human, demonstrating the near-universal nature of the genetic code.

questions.question: Which codon has dual functions - coding for Methionine and acting as an initiator codon?
questions.explanation: AUG has dual functions. It codes for Methionine (met), and it also acts as initiator codon.

questions.question: Which of the following are stop terminator codons?
questions.explanation: UAA, UAG, and UGA are stop terminator codons that signal the end of protein synthesis.

questions.question: What was George Gamow's profession?
questions.explanation: George Gamow was a physicist who proposed the triplet nature of the genetic code.

questions.question: Why was the proposition and deciphering of genetic code considered most challenging?
options: It required involvement of scientists from several disciplines
It was solved by a single scientist
questions.explanation: The proposition and deciphering of genetic code required involvement of scientists from several disciplines including physicists, organic chemists, biochemists and geneticists.

questions.question: What type of RNA molecules did Khorana synthesise?
questions.explanation: Har Gobind Khorana synthesised RNA molecules with defined combinations of bases including homopolymers and copolymers.

questions.question: What does the term 'degenerate' mean in the context of genetic code?
options: The code is broken or damaged
Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon
The code is different in every organism
questions.explanation: Degenerate means that some amino acids are coded by more than one codon, providing redundancy in the genetic code.

questions.question: What is the nature of the genetic code regarding its universality?
options: Nearly universal with some exceptions in mitochondrial codons and protozoans
questions.explanation: The code is nearly universal from bacteria to human, but some exceptions have been found in mitochondrial codons and in some protozoans.

questions.question: How many stop codons are there in the genetic code?
questions.explanation: There are 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) that do not code for any amino acids.

questions.question: What is the total number of possible codons in the genetic code?
questions.explanation: The total number of possible codons is 64, generated by 4^3 permutation combination of the four bases.

questions.question: What does AUG code for?
questions.explanation: AUG codes for Methionine (met) and also acts as the initiator codon.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of the genetic code?
options: The code has punctuation marks between codons
questions.explanation: The codon is read in a contiguous fashion with no punctuations. There are no punctuation marks between codons.

questions.question: What was the role of polynucleotide phosphorylase in deciphering the genetic code?
options: It polymerised RNA with defined sequences in a template-independent manner
questions.explanation: Polynucleotide phosphorylase (Severo Ochoa enzyme) polymerised RNA with defined sequences in a template-independent manner, aiding in enzymatic synthesis of RNA.

questions.question: What does the term 'contiguous' mean in the context of genetic code reading?
options: Codons are read continuously without gaps or punctuation
Codons are read from different mRNAs
questions.explanation: Contiguous means the codon is read continuously in mRNA without any gaps or punctuation marks between codons.

questions.question: When was the Human Genome Project launched?
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project was launched in the year 1990. It was a 13-year project coordinated by the U.S. Department of Energy and the National Institute of Health.

questions.question: What is the approximate size of the human genome in base pairs?
questions.explanation: The human genome is said to have approximately 3 x 10^9 base pairs. This enormous size made the project a mega project requiring massive resources.

questions.question: Which organizations coordinated the Human Genome Project?
options: U.S. Department of Energy and National Institute of Health
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project was coordinated by the U.S. Department of Energy and the National Institute of Health. The Wellcome Trust (U.K.) became a major partner during the early years.

questions.question: In which year was the Human Genome Project completed?
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project was completed in 2003. It was a 13-year project that started in 1990.

questions.question: What was the estimated cost of sequencing per base pair at the beginning of the project?
questions.explanation: The estimated cost of sequencing at the beginning of the project was US $3 per base pair. With approximately 3 x 10^9 bp, the total estimated cost would be approximately 9 billion US dollars.

questions.question: Which of the following countries contributed to the Human Genome Project?
options: United States, United Kingdom, Japan, France, Germany, and China
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project received contributions from multiple countries including the United States, United Kingdom (Wellcome Trust), Japan, France, Germany, and China.

questions.question: How many books would be required to store the DNA sequence from a single human cell if each page contained 1000 letters and each book contained 1000 pages?
questions.explanation: If each page contained 1000 letters and each book contained 1000 pages, then 3300 such books would be required to store the information of DNA sequence from a single human cell. This illustrates the enormous amount of data generated by the project.

questions.question: What is one of the primary goals of the Human Genome Project?
options: To create new species of organisms
To identify all approximately 20,000-25,000 genes in human DNA
questions.explanation: One of the important goals of the Human Genome Project was to identify all the approximately 20,000-25,000 genes in human DNA. Other goals included determining the sequences of the 3 billion chemical base pairs and storing this information in databases.

questions.question: What does ELSI stand for in the context of the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: ELSI stands for Ethical, Legal, and Social Issues. Addressing these issues was one of the goals of the Human Genome Project as genetic information raises important ethical and legal concerns.

questions.question: What new area in biology developed rapidly in association with the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project was closely associated with the rapid development of a new area in biology called Bioinformatics. The enormous amount of data necessitated the use of high speed computational devices for data storage, retrieval, and analysis.

questions.question: What was the approximate number of base pairs in the human genome according to the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: The human genome contains approximately 3 x 10^9 base pairs. This was one of the key figures mentioned in the Human Genome Project description.

questions.question: What was the estimated cost per base pair for sequencing at the beginning of the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: The cost of sequencing was estimated at US $3 per base pair at the beginning of the Human Genome Project.

questions.question: What was the total estimated cost of the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: With approximately 3 x 10^9 bp at $3 per bp, the total estimated cost was approximately 9 billion US dollars.

questions.question: How many books would be required to store the DNA sequence information from a single human cell if each book had 1000 pages with 1000 letters per page?
questions.explanation: 3300 books would be required to store the DNA sequence from a single human cell, given 3 x 10^9 base pairs and 1000 letters per page across 1000 pages per book.

questions.question: Which new area in biology was closely associated with the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: Bioinformatics was the new area in biology that developed rapidly in association with the Human Genome Project for data storage, retrieval, and analysis.

questions.question: What was the approximate range of genes the Human Genome Project aimed to identify in human DNA?
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project aimed to identify approximately 20,000-25,000 genes in human DNA.

questions.question: How many chemical base pairs make up human DNA according to the Human Genome Project goals?
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project aimed to determine the sequences of 3 billion chemical base pairs that make up human DNA.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT listed as a goal of the Human Genome Project?
options: Identify all genes in human DNA
questions.explanation: Cloning human beings was not listed as a goal. The goals included identifying genes, storing information, improving tools, transferring technologies, and addressing ethical issues.

questions.question: What does ELSI stand for in the context of Human Genome Project goals?
questions.explanation: ELSI stands for Ethical, Legal, and Social Issues that may arise from the Human Genome Project.

questions.question: How long was the Human Genome Project planned to run?
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project was a 13-year project coordinated by the U.S. Department of Energy and the National Institute of Health.

questions.question: Which UK organization became a major partner during the early years of the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: The Wellcome Trust (U.K.) became a major partner during the early years of the Human Genome Project.

questions.question: In which year was the Human Genome Project completed?
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project was completed in 2003.

questions.question: Which of the following countries contributed to the Human Genome Project?
options: United States, United Kingdom, Japan, France, Germany, and China
questions.explanation: Contributions came from the U.S., U.K. (Wellcome Trust), Japan, France, Germany, China and others.

questions.question: What are Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs) in the context of Human Genome Project methodologies?
options: DNA sequences that are not expressed
Genes that are expressed as RNA
questions.explanation: ESTs are identified genes that are expressed as RNA. This was one of the two major approaches used in the Human Genome Project.

questions.question: What is Sequence Annotation in the context of Human Genome Project methodologies?
options: Assigning functions to different regions in the sequence
questions.explanation: Sequence Annotation refers to assigning different regions in the sequence with functions after sequencing the whole genome.

questions.question: What were BAC and YAC used as in the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: BAC (bacterial artificial chromosomes) and YAC (yeast artificial chromosomes) were used as vectors for cloning DNA fragments in suitable hosts.

questions.question: Which organisms were commonly used as hosts for cloning DNA fragments in the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: Bacteria and yeast were the commonly used hosts for cloning DNA fragments in the Human Genome Project.

questions.question: Who developed the method used by automated DNA sequencers in the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: Frederick Sanger developed the method used by automated DNA sequencers. He is also credited for developing the method for determination of amino acid sequences in proteins.

questions.question: When was the sequence of chromosome 1 completed?
questions.explanation: The sequence of chromosome 1 was completed in May 2006, which was the last of the 24 human chromosomes to be sequenced.

questions.question: How many human chromosomes were sequenced in the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: 24 human chromosomes were sequenced: 22 autosomes and X and Y chromosomes.

questions.question: What were used to generate genetic and physical maps on the genome?
options: Polymorphism of restriction endonuclease recognition sites and microsatellites
questions.explanation: Genetic and physical maps were generated using information on polymorphism of restriction endonuclease recognition sites and repetitive DNA sequences known as microsatellites.

questions.question: What is a microsatellite?
questions.explanation: Microsatellites are repetitive DNA sequences that were used in generating genetic and physical maps on the genome.

questions.question: What was the purpose of converting total DNA into random fragments of smaller sizes?
options: To overcome technical limitations in sequencing very long DNA pieces
questions.explanation: DNA was converted into random fragments of smaller sizes because there are technical limitations in sequencing very long pieces of DNA.

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-human model organism that was sequenced in the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: Caenorhabditis elegans, a free living non-pathogenic nematode, was one of the non-human model organisms sequenced.

questions.question: What was the main reason for calling the Human Genome Project a mega project?
options: It was very small in scope
It required enormous resources, time, and data management capabilities
questions.explanation: The HGP was called a mega project because of its enormous magnitude, requirements, cost (approximately 9 billion dollars), and the need for high-speed computational devices for data management.

questions.question: What was the estimated cost of the Human Genome Project if sequencing cost $3 per base pair?
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project aimed to sequence approximately 3 billion base pairs. At $3 per base pair, the total estimated cost was approximately 9 billion US dollars.

questions.question: Which two organizations coordinated the Human Genome Project?
options: U.S. Department of Energy and National Institute of Health
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project was a 13-year project coordinated by the U.S. Department of Energy and the National Institute of Health.

questions.question: In which year was the Human Genome Project completed?
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project was completed in 2003.

questions.question: What does EST stand for in the context of the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: EST stands for Expressed Sequence Tags, which are RNA sequences that are expressed as genes. This was one of the two major approaches used in the Human Genome Project.

questions.question: Which method was used for DNA sequencing in the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: The fragments were sequenced using automated DNA sequencers that worked on the principle of a method developed by Frederick Sanger.

questions.question: What are BAC and YAC used for in the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: BAC (Bacterial Artificial Chromosomes) and YAC (Yeast Artificial Chromosomes) were used as vectors to clone DNA fragments in suitable hosts like bacteria and yeast.

questions.question: When was the sequence of chromosome 1 completed?
questions.explanation: The sequence of chromosome 1 was completed in May 2006, which was the last of the 24 human chromosomes to be sequenced.

questions.question: How many human chromosomes were sequenced in the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project sequenced 24 human chromosomes: 22 autosomes and the X and Y chromosomes.

questions.question: What is sequence annotation in the context of the Human Genome Project?
options: Assigning functions to different regions in the sequence
questions.explanation: Sequence annotation refers to assigning different regions in the sequence with functions after sequencing the whole genome.

questions.question: Which country became a major partner during the early years of the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: During the early years of the HGP, the Wellcome Trust (U.K.) became a major partner.

questions.question: What is the purpose of generating overlapping DNA fragments in the Human Genome Project?
options: To arrange sequences based on overlapping regions
questions.explanation: Overlapping fragments were generated so that the sequences could be arranged based on overlapping regions present in them. This alignment was done using specialized computer-based programs.

questions.question: What are microsatellites used for in the Human Genome Project?
options: Assigning genetic and physical maps on the genome
questions.explanation: Microsatellites are repetitive DNA sequences used for assigning genetic and physical maps on the genome, along with restriction endonuclease recognition site polymorphism.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a goal of the Human Genome Project?
options: Determine sequences of 3 billion base pairs
questions.explanation: Creating genetically modified humans was not a goal of the Human Genome Project. The goals included identifying genes, determining base pair sequences, storing information, improving data analysis tools, and addressing ethical issues.

questions.question: How many books would be required to store the DNA sequence from a single human cell if each page contains 1000 letters and each book contains 1000 pages?
questions.explanation: If each page contains 1000 letters and each book contains 1000 pages, then 3300 such books would be required to store the information of DNA sequence from a single human cell.

questions.question: What does ELSI stand for in the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: ELSI stands for Ethical, Legal, and Social Issues, which the Human Genome Project aimed to address.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a non-human model organism sequenced in the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: Elephant was not mentioned as a model organism. The text mentions bacteria, yeast, Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila, rice, and Arabidopsis as model organisms.

questions.question: What was the primary reason for cloning DNA fragments before sequencing?
options: To amplify each piece for easier sequencing
questions.explanation: Cloning resulted in amplification of each DNA fragment so that it could subsequently be sequenced with ease.

questions.question: What type of DNA sequences are microsatellites?
questions.explanation: Microsatellites are repetitive DNA sequences that show polymorphism and are used for genetic mapping.

questions.question: What is the significance of the Human Genome Project for understanding human biology?
options: It provides clues to understanding human biology
It only helps in energy production
questions.explanation: The Human Genome Project provides clues to understanding human biology and also helps in understanding non-human organisms for applications in healthcare, agriculture, energy production, and environmental remediation.

questions.question: Which technique was used to separate DNA fragments of different sizes in the Human Genome Project?
questions.explanation: Electrophoresis was used to separate DNA fragments by size, which is a standard technique in DNA analysis.

questions.question: In Griffith's experiment with Streptococcus pneumoniae, which strain was virulent and caused pneumonia in mice?
questions.explanation: The S strain (smooth) bacteria had a mucous polysaccharide coat and were virulent, causing pneumonia in mice. The R strain (rough) lacked this coat and was non-virulent.

questions.question: What happened when heat-killed S strain bacteria were injected into mice?
options: The mice transformed into S strain carriers
questions.explanation: Heat-killed S strain bacteria did not kill the mice because the bacteria were dead and could not cause infection.

questions.question: What was Griffith's conclusion when mice died after being injected with a mixture of heat-killed S and live R bacteria?
options: A transforming principle from heat-killed S strain transformed R strain into virulent S strain
The heat-killed S strain revived and multiplied
The mice had natural immunity against R strain only
questions.explanation: Griffith concluded that some transforming principle was transferred from heat-killed S strain to live R strain, enabling R strain to synthesize a smooth polysaccharide coat and become virulent.

questions.question: Which enzymes did Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty use to prove that DNA is the transforming principle?
questions.explanation: They used proteases (protein-digesting) and RNases (RNA-digesting) which did not affect transformation, but DNase (DNA-digesting) inhibited transformation, proving DNA is the genetic material.

questions.question: In the Hershey-Chase experiment, which radioactive isotope was used to label DNA?
questions.explanation: Radioactive phosphorus (32P) was used to label DNA because DNA contains phosphorus in its phosphate groups. Protein does not contain phosphorus.

questions.question: What was the key finding of the Hershey-Chase experiment after blending and centrifugation?
options: Radioactive proteins entered the bacterial cells
Radioactive DNA entered the bacterial cells
Both DNA and proteins entered the bacterial cells
Neither DNA nor proteins entered the bacterial cells
questions.explanation: Bacteria infected with 32P-labeled DNA were radioactive, indicating DNA passed from virus to bacteria. Bacteria with 35S-labeled protein were not radioactive, showing proteins did not enter.

questions.question: What characteristic of the S strain made it appear smooth and shiny on culture plates?
options: Presence of a mucous polysaccharide coat
Presence of a thick peptidoglycan layer
questions.explanation: The S strain bacteria produced smooth shiny colonies because they had a mucous polysaccharide coat. The R strain lacked this coat and appeared rough.

questions.question: Before Avery's work, what was commonly believed to be the genetic material?
questions.explanation: Prior to Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty's work, proteins were thought to be the genetic material due to their complexity and variety.

questions.question: What effect did DNase have on the transforming principle in Avery's experiment?
options: It had no effect on transformation
questions.explanation: Digestion with DNase inhibited transformation, suggesting that DNA was the transforming substance. This was crucial evidence that DNA is the genetic material.

questions.question: What type of viruses did Hershey and Chase use in their experiment?
questions.explanation: Hershey and Chase worked with bacteriophages, which are viruses that infect bacteria. These viruses attach to bacteria and inject their genetic material.

questions.question: Why was radioactive sulfur (35S) used in the Hershey-Chase experiment?
options: Because protein contains sulfur but DNA does not
Because both DNA and protein contain sulfur
Because sulfur is a component of nucleotides
questions.explanation: Radioactive sulfur was used because sulfur is present in proteins (in amino acids like cysteine and methionine) but absent in DNA. This allowed specific labeling of protein.

questions.question: What happened when live R strain bacteria were injected into mice?
options: The mice survived and did not develop pneumonia
The mice became carriers of both R and S strains
questions.explanation: Mice infected with the live R strain did not develop pneumonia and survived because the R strain lacked the protective mucous coat and was non-virulent.

questions.question: Which experiment provided the unequivocal proof that DNA is the genetic material?
questions.explanation: Hershey and Chase's 1952 experiment provided the unequivocal proof that DNA is the genetic material by showing that only DNA entered bacteria during viral infection.

questions.question: What was the purpose of using a blender in the Hershey-Chase experiment?
options: To break down bacterial cell walls
To separate viral protein coats from bacteria
To mix the radioactive isotopes evenly
questions.explanation: The blender was used to agitate and remove the viral protein coats from the surface of bacteria after infection, allowing separation of coats from bacterial cells.

questions.question: In the Hershey-Chase experiment, what did centrifugation achieve?
options: It separated virus particles from bacteria
It mixed DNA and proteins together
questions.explanation: Centrifugation separated the heavier bacterial cells from the lighter virus particles, allowing researchers to determine which radioactive component entered the bacteria.

questions.question: Which property of DNA made it a better candidate for genetic material than protein?
options: DNA is more complex than protein
DNA can replicate and is structurally stable
DNA has more types of monomers than protein
DNA is larger than protein molecules
questions.explanation: DNA can generate its replica through replication and is chemically and structurally stable, making it suitable for storing genetic information.

questions.question: In bacteria, how many major types of RNA are needed for protein synthesis?
questions.explanation: In bacteria, there are three major types of RNAs: mRNA (messenger RNA), tRNA (transfer RNA), and rRNA (ribosomal RNA). All three are essential for protein synthesis. The mRNA provides the template, tRNA brings amino acids and reads the genetic code, and rRNAs play structural and catalytic roles during translation.

questions.question: Which enzyme catalyzes transcription of all types of RNA in bacteria?
questions.explanation: There is a single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase that catalyzes transcription of all types of RNA in bacteria. This enzyme binds to the promoter and initiates transcription, using nucleoside triphosphates as substrate.

questions.question: What does the sigma factor do during bacterial transcription?
options: It initiates transcription by helping RNA polymerase recognize the promoter
It adds poly-A tail to mRNA
questions.explanation: The sigma factor is an initiation factor that associates transiently with RNA polymerase to help it recognize and bind to the promoter region. It alters the specificity of RNA polymerase to initiate transcription. After initiation, the sigma factor dissociates.

questions.question: Which factor is responsible for termination of transcription in bacteria?
questions.explanation: The Rho factor is a termination factor that associates with RNA polymerase to terminate transcription. When the polymerase reaches the terminator region, the nascent RNA falls off along with the RNA polymerase, resulting in termination.

questions.question: Why can transcription and translation be coupled in bacteria?
options: Because bacteria have a nuclear membrane
Because there is no separation between transcription and translation compartments
Because bacterial mRNA requires extensive processing
questions.explanation: In bacteria, transcription and translation take place in the same compartment because there is no separation of cytosol and nucleus. The mRNA does not require processing to become active, so translation can begin before the mRNA is fully transcribed.

questions.question: Which RNA polymerase in eukaryotes transcribes rRNAs (28S, 18S, and 5.8S)?
questions.explanation: In eukaryotes, RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNAs (28S, 18S, and 5.8S). RNA polymerase II transcribes precursor of mRNA (hnRNA), and RNA polymerase III is responsible for transcription of tRNA, 5S rRNA, and snRNAs.

questions.question: What is the process called when introns are removed and exons are joined in eukaryotic mRNA?
questions.explanation: Splicing is the process where introns (intervening sequences) are removed and exons (expressed sequences) are joined in a defined order. This produces functional mRNA from the primary transcript that contains both exons and introns.

questions.question: What is added to the 5' end of hnRNA during capping in eukaryotes?
questions.explanation: In capping, an unusual nucleotide called methyl guanosine triphosphate is added to the 5'-end of hnRNA. This cap protects the mRNA from degradation and helps in ribosome binding during translation.

questions.question: How many adenylate residues are typically added during tailing of eukaryotic mRNA?
questions.explanation: During tailing, adenylate residues (200-300) are added at the 3'-end of hnRNA in a template-independent manner. This poly-A tail helps in mRNA stability and export from the nucleus.

questions.question: What is the fully processed hnRNA called after capping, tailing, and splicing in eukaryotes?
questions.explanation: The fully processed hnRNA, after undergoing capping, tailing, and splicing, is called mRNA (messenger RNA). This mature mRNA is then transported out of the nucleus for translation.

questions.question: Who performed the experiment that proved DNA replicates semiconservatively in 1958?
questions.explanation: Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl performed the experiment in 1958 that proved DNA replicates semiconservatively. They used E. coli grown in heavy nitrogen (15N) medium and then transferred to normal nitrogen (14N) medium.

questions.question: What isotope of nitrogen was used as the heavy nitrogen source in Meselson and Stahl's experiment?
questions.explanation: 15N (heavy isotope of nitrogen) was used as the nitrogen source in the form of 15NH4Cl. This heavy nitrogen gets incorporated into newly synthesized DNA.

questions.question: How was the heavy DNA distinguished from normal DNA in the Meselson and Stahl experiment?
options: By centrifugation in cesium chloride density gradient
questions.explanation: The heavy DNA molecule was distinguished from normal DNA by centrifugation in a cesium chloride (CsCl) density gradient. 15N is not radioactive, so it can only be separated based on density differences.

questions.question: What was the density of DNA extracted after one generation (20 minutes) when E. coli was transferred from 15N to 14N medium?
questions.explanation: After one generation (20 minutes), the DNA extracted had a hybrid or intermediate density because it contained one strand of heavy DNA (15N) and one strand of light DNA (14N).

questions.question: What was the composition of DNA after two generations (40 minutes) in the Meselson and Stahl experiment?
options: Equal amounts of hybrid DNA and light DNA
Equal amounts of heavy DNA and light DNA
questions.explanation: After two generations (40 minutes), the DNA was composed of equal amounts of hybrid DNA (one 15N strand and one 14N strand) and light DNA (both 14N strands).

questions.question: Which plant was used by Taylor and colleagues in 1958 to prove semiconservative DNA replication in chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Taylor and colleagues performed experiments on Vicia faba (faba beans) using radioactive thymidine to detect distribution of newly synthesized DNA in chromosomes, proving semiconservative replication.

questions.question: What technique did Taylor use to detect newly synthesized DNA in chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Taylor and colleagues used radioactive thymidine to detect the distribution of newly synthesized DNA in chromosomes during their experiments on Vicia faba.

questions.question: If E. coli was allowed to grow for 80 minutes in 14N medium after being in 15N medium, what would be the proportions of light and hybrid DNA?
options: More light DNA than hybrid DNA
Equal amounts of light and hybrid DNA
questions.explanation: After 80 minutes (4 generations), the proportion would be more light DNA than hybrid DNA. In each generation, the number of light DNA molecules doubles while hybrid DNA remains constant. After 4 generations: 14 light DNA and 2 hybrid DNA molecules.

questions.question: Which direction does DNA-dependent DNA polymerase catalyse polymerisation?
questions.explanation: DNA-dependent DNA polymerases catalyse polymerisation only in the 5' to 3' direction. This creates complications at the replication fork because the two template strands have opposite polarities.

questions.question: On which template strand is DNA replication continuous?
questions.explanation: On the template strand with 3' to 5' polarity, replication is continuous because the new strand can be synthesised in the 5' to 3' direction continuously. This is called the leading strand.

questions.question: What are the discontinuously synthesised DNA fragments called?
questions.explanation: The discontinuously synthesised fragments on the lagging strand are called Okazaki fragments. They are later joined by DNA ligase to form a continuous strand.

questions.question: What is the function of DNA ligase in replication?
options: Adds nucleotides to the growing strand
questions.explanation: DNA ligase joins the discontinuously synthesised Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand by forming phosphodiester bonds between them.

questions.question: What is the specific region where replication originates called?
questions.explanation: The origin of replication is a definite region in DNA where replication initiates. DNA polymerases cannot initiate replication randomly at any place.

questions.question: How long does E. coli take to complete DNA replication?
questions.explanation: E. coli completes the process of replication within 18 minutes. It has 4.6 x 10^6 base pairs, requiring an average rate of approximately 2000 bp per second.

questions.question: In which phase of the cell cycle does DNA replication occur in eukaryotes?
questions.explanation: In eukaryotes, DNA replication takes place during the S-phase (synthesis phase) of the cell cycle. This is when the cell duplicates its DNA content.

questions.question: What chromosomal anomaly results from failure in cell division after DNA replication?
questions.explanation: A failure in cell division after DNA replication results in polyploidy, a chromosomal anomaly where cells contain multiple sets of chromosomes.

questions.question: What dual purpose do deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates serve during replication?
questions.explanation: Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates serve dual purposes: they act as substrates for polymerisation and provide energy for the reaction through their two terminal high-energy phosphates.

questions.question: What is the small opening of the DNA helix where replication occurs called?
questions.explanation: The replication fork is the small opening of the DNA helix where replication occurs. Since the two strands cannot be separated in their entire length due to high energy requirements, replication occurs within this opening.

questions.question: What is the process of copying genetic information from one strand of DNA into RNA called?
questions.explanation: Transcription is the process of copying genetic information from one strand of DNA into RNA. During this process, the principle of complementarity governs, but adenosine pairs with uracil instead of thymine.

questions.question: In transcription, which nitrogenous base pairs with adenine instead of thymine?
questions.explanation: During transcription, adenosine forms a base pair with uracil instead of thymine. This is a key difference between DNA replication and transcription.

questions.question: Unlike replication, what happens to the DNA during transcription?
options: Only a segment of DNA and one strand is copied into RNA
questions.explanation: Unlike replication where the total DNA of an organism gets duplicated, in transcription only a segment of DNA and only one of the strands is copied into RNA. This requires defining boundaries for the region and strand to be transcribed.

questions.question: Why are both strands of DNA not copied during transcription?
options: It would produce identical RNA molecules
It would complicate genetic information transfer and form double-stranded RNA
RNA polymerase cannot bind to both strands
It would require too much energy
questions.explanation: If both strands act as templates, they would code for RNA molecules with different sequences, leading to different proteins and complicating genetic information transfer. Also, the two complementary RNA molecules would form double-stranded RNA, preventing translation into protein.

questions.question: What are the three regions that define a transcription unit in DNA?
questions.explanation: A transcription unit in DNA is defined by three primary regions: (i) A Promoter, (ii) The Structural gene, and (iii) A Terminator. These regions work together to control the transcription process.

questions.question: Which strand of DNA acts as the template strand during transcription?
questions.explanation: The strand that has the polarity 3' to 5' acts as the template strand during transcription. RNA polymerase catalyzes polymerization in the 5' to 3' direction, so it reads the template strand from 3' to 5'.

questions.question: What is the coding strand also known as?
questions.explanation: The coding strand has the polarity 5' to 3' and the sequence same as RNA (except thymine at the place of uracil). It is also referred to as the sense strand. The template strand is also called the antisense strand.

questions.question: Where is the promoter located in relation to the structural gene?
options: Towards the 3' end (downstream) of the coding strand
Towards the 5' end (upstream) of the structural gene
questions.explanation: The promoter is located towards the 5' end (upstream) of the structural gene, with reference to the polarity of the coding strand. It provides the binding site for RNA polymerase and defines the template and coding strands.

questions.question: What would happen if both DNA strands were transcribed simultaneously?
options: Formation of double-stranded RNA preventing translation
questions.explanation: If both strands were transcribed, the two RNA molecules produced would be complementary to each other and would form double-stranded RNA. This would prevent RNA from being translated into protein, making transcription futile.

questions.question: Which enzyme catalyzes polymerization during transcription?
questions.explanation: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the polymerization of nucleotides during transcription. It reads the template strand and synthesizes RNA in the 5' to 3' direction.

questions.question: What is the direction of RNA polymerase activity during transcription?
questions.explanation: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes polymerization only in one direction, that is 5' to 3'. This is why the template strand must be read from 3' to 5' for proper RNA synthesis.

questions.question: What happens to the coding strand during transcription?
options: It is used as the template
It is displaced and not used for coding
questions.explanation: The coding strand is displaced during transcription. It has the same sequence as RNA (except thymine instead of uracil) and does not code for anything directly, but serves as a reference point for defining the transcription unit.

questions.question: Where is the terminator located in a transcription unit?
options: Towards the 5' end of the coding strand
Towards the 3' end (downstream) of the coding strand
questions.explanation: The terminator is located towards the 3' end (downstream) of the coding strand and usually defines the end of the transcription process. It works together with the promoter to flank the structural gene.

questions.question: What additional sequences may be present near the promoter in a transcription unit?
questions.explanation: There are additional regulatory sequences that may be present further upstream or downstream to the promoter. These sequences play roles in regulating gene expression and will be discussed in the section on regulation of gene expression.

questions.question: In the given example, what is the sequence of the template strand?
questions.explanation: The template strand has the polarity 3' to 5' and the sequence 3'-ATGCATGCATGCATGCATGCATGC-5'. This strand is read by RNA polymerase to synthesize complementary RNA.

questions.question: What is the relationship between the coding strand and the RNA sequence?
options: They have the same sequence except T is replaced by U
They are complementary to each other
The coding strand is longer than the RNA
questions.explanation: The coding strand has the same sequence as the RNA produced during transcription, except that thymine (T) in DNA is replaced by uracil (U) in RNA. This is why it is called the coding strand.

questions.question: A transcription unit in DNA is defined by how many primary regions?
questions.explanation: A transcription unit in DNA is defined primarily by three regions: (i) A Promoter, (ii) The Structural gene, and (iii) A Terminator.

questions.question: Which strand of DNA acts as the template during transcription?
questions.explanation: The strand that has the polarity 3'-5' acts as a template and is referred to as the template strand. The DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes polymerization in the 5'-3' direction, so it reads the template strand in the 3'-5' direction.

questions.question: What is the coding strand also called during transcription?
questions.explanation: The coding strand has the polarity 5'-3' and the sequence same as RNA (except thymine at the place of uracil). It is also referred to as the sense strand. The template strand is sometimes called the antisense strand.

questions.question: Where is the promoter located with respect to the structural gene?
questions.explanation: The promoter is located towards the 5'-end (upstream) of the structural gene. The reference is made with respect to the polarity of the coding strand. The terminator is located towards the 3'-end (downstream).
